pages.text: FU is denominated $(l)by tier$(): a Tier 5 spool stores Tier 5 FU, a Tier 1 spool stores Tier 1 FU. One unit of Tier N FU is worth several units of Tier N-1 (the $(l)conversion ratio$(), set in config).$(br2)So the tier of a spool isn't just capacity — each unit is intrinsically more valuable the higher you go.

pages.title: Where FU Cost Comes From
pages.text: Each block's FU cost — and its tier — is $(l)derived from its recipe graph$(): crafting, plus optionally smelting and stonecutting. A diamond block costs what its diamonds are worth; stone costs almost nothing.$(br2)A block's material tier sets the minimum machine and spool tier needed to print it, so cheap blocks stay cheap and rare blocks stay gated.

pages.title: Winding vs Spending
pages.text: Two different rules, by design:$(br)$(li)$(l)Winding$() (making FU) is $(l)exact-tier$(): netherite only winds into a T5 spool$(li)$(l)Spending$() (printing) is $(l)down-only$(): a spool pays any cost at or below its tier, never above$(br2)Together these stop cobblestone-farming from ever reaching a high-tier spool, while letting your best spools print anything below them.

pages.title: Lower Tiers Cost More
pages.text: Lower-tier machines are deliberately less efficient — a Tier 1 printer pays a higher FU multiplier per block than a Tier 8 Fabricator.$(br2)Climbing the tiers isn't just about bigger prints: every tier you gain makes the same structure $(l)cheaper$() to print. The full ratio and per-tier efficiencies are in the config for pack makers.
